title: Forever Charmed by V brings permanent jewelry and community spirit to Bay Ridge - Brooklyn Paper
content: A new small business is adding sparkle to Bay Ridge. Forever Charmed by V, a permanent jewelry studio owned by Vanessa Dedos, officially opened its doors on May 7 just off Fifth Avenue and 77th Street. The shop specializes in custom-fitted permanent jewelry while also showcasing products from local makers at the Side Street Boutique, creating a space that blends personalized accessories with neighborhood collaboration. Dedos’s journey to opening her own storefront began nearly four years ago when she launched the business through private events, pop-ups, markets and parties. When she had the opportunity to open a permanent space, it felt like a natural extension. “I started doing those events at another local shop here in Bay Ridge,” she told Brooklyn Paper. “It really took off from there.” The new storefront was designed with both customers and the community in mind. While still an intimate space, the studio can comfortably accommodate groups of five to eight people at a time. Forever Charmed by V visitors can also browse stocked shelves with products from local artisans, including rings, earrings, perfumes and bags. “We built this with the intention of being able to have morepeople come in at a time,” Dedos said. “And the local makers’ products on the shelves bring a great variety.” Although permanent jewelry has become increasingly popular across the country, Dedos said many New Yorkers are unfamiliar with the concept. “It’s funny because I have a lot of people still asking what permanent jewelry is,” she laughed. The process is simple and highly personalized. Customers choose a chain, select optional charms and have the piece custom-fitted to their wrist, finger or ankle before it is welded closed. While traditional permanent jewelry is designed to work continuously without a clasp, the shop now offers clasp options as well for customers who want greater flexibility. After just a month in its new location, Dedos said the neighborhood has embraced the business. “The community has been great,” she said. “We’ve been living here going on eight or nine years, and it really does feel like a community here. Everyone supports each other, and they show up at events, and it’s amazing.” That sense of community is part of what drew her to Bay Ridge and what she hopes to foster through the shop. “It’s a feeling you typically don’t get in the city, but it is really nice.” For Dedos, the most rewarding part of the business is seeing customers leave happy with their new jewelry. “I love it because it’s fun. and I truly enjoy watching people love their pieces in the end,” she said. “I love the flexibility and schedule it offers — I’m a mom and a wife — and I enjoy just having a business.” Her attention to detail is reflected in the personalized experience she offers, helping customers select chains and create pieces tailored to their style and a welcome sign with their name on it upon entry. Forever Charmed by V will celebrate its official grand opening on June 20 from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. with a community event featuring local vendors and artists. Guests can enjoy coffee from Bark & Brew Coffee, a husband-and-wife coffee cart from Park Slope, and treats from Bay Ridge cookie business Sweet Streets of Brooklyn. The event will also feature customized luggage tag art by Danielle Rose Fisher, meet-and-greets with makers whose products are sold in the shop, a lemonade and baked goods stand run by local children and, of course, permanent jewelry. “It’s this really sweet lineup,” Dedos said. “It’’s a little but of everything to day, ‘Hello, we’re here!’” Forever Charmed by V is open Wednesdays through Fridays from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m., Saturdays from 12 p.m. to 6 p.m. and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m. For more information, visit their Instagram. Olivia Seaman is a reporter for Brooklyn Paper, where she covers all things Brooklyn — from neighborhood news and local politics to culture, community voices and the everyday stories that help shape the borough. title: Fraunhofer ISE achieves 34.4 efficiency for III-V germanium solar module - pv magazine Global
content: Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE announced it was able to increase the power conversion efficiency of its record-breaking III-V germanium solar module from 34.2% to 34.4%. “Compared to the previous record of 34,2% the thing we changed was the layout,” Fraunhofe ISE scientist Laura Stevens told pv magazine. “We used the same cell technology and the same front side glass type. The first module had shingle strings and in the second, better module we connected the cells in a shingle matrix.” The result was achieved using “shingle-matrix” technology in combination with space-grade solar cells, the German institute said. The previous record of 34.2% was set earlier this year using an 833 cm² module also based on space-grade solar cells from Azur Space. For the latest development, the cell manufacturer adapted its triple-junction solar cell technology to the terrestrial solar spectrum. The anti-reflective front glass structures used for the module were supplied by Temicon. A key factor in the new record is the use of shingle-matrix technology for interconnecting the solar cells. Developed by Fraunhofer ISE in cooperation with a mechanical engineering partner, the approach is now also used in commercial module manufacturing. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, arranged in an overlapping shingle pattern, and bonded with electrically conductive adhesive (ECA). This enables direct cell-to-cell contact, eliminates solder-coated copper ribbons, reduces shading, and increases active area utilization. title: U.S. Supreme Court strikes down ban on interracial marriage on June 12, 1967 - KNOE
content: MONROE, La. (KNOE) - On June 12, 1967 the United States Supreme Court issued a ruling that would strike down any ban on interracial marriage. The case was Loving v. Virginia, and the subject was Virginia’s Racial Integrity Act. Two Virginia residents, Richard Loving and Mildred Jeter, were married in Washington, D.C. in June of 1958 where there was no ban. Richard was white, Mildred was black. They returned to their home state of Virginia and established a home in Caroline County. That October, a grand jury issued an indictment on the Lovings charging them with violating the Virginia Racial Integrity Act. The couple pleaded guilty and were sentenced to a year in prison. The trial judge suspended their sentence on the condition the Lovings leave Virginia and not return together for 25 years. Mr. and Mrs. Loving moved to the District of Columbia. On November 6, 1963, they filed a motion in state court saying the judgement had violated their rights under the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. When no decision had been made by October, 1964, they started a class action suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. When the state trial judge refused to throw out their sentences, they continued their appeals until it reached the United States Supreme Court. On June 12, 1967, the Supreme Court handed down the ruling that the Lovings’ convictions must be reversed. Their unanimous decision included this opinion: “These statutes also deprive the Lovings of liberty without due process of law in violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The freedom to marry has long been recognized as one of the vital personal rights essential to the orderly pursuit of happiness by free men.” “The Fourteenth Amendment requires that the freedom of choice to marry not be restricted by invidious racial discriminations. Under our Constitution, the freedom to marry, or not marry, a person of another race resides with the individual, and cannot be infringed by the State.”

title: Gig Review: Greetings V At Vespers - Still Listening Magazine
content:
It’s hard to make Vespers sing. The club space, formerly Peckham Audio, is a classic London high street basement sinkhole - broken ceramics and sticky floors paired typically with a baﬄing array of acts. Over its tenure, the venue (under both names) has hosted Dean Blunt, bod [包家巷], Jane Fitz, Krautrock Karaoke, Evicshen, John Maus, L-VIS 1990, GFOTY, Tek Lintowe, Jackzebra, and so many others. Shows which tend towards inviting the mesmeric chaos you’d associate with 3 cans too many. Squeezed amongst a Tonkotsu franchise and the tragically disappearing legacy shops of the Rye Lane shopping centre, it’s vital that a venue is still chipping away at the brick wall of live music economics, but it can also feel like the graft required to pull oﬀ this magic trick produces a frayed and diﬃcult venue experience for the occasional punter. It’s held together by the grit and passion of its staﬀ, and you can feel the knife’s edge in the lovecraftian terror of the toilets and the moderate jank of a ‘green room’ tucked behind a black polyester curtain. It’s not a place I’d have had in mind for a sensitive Thursday evening of live performances as a heatwave crested the capital, but Greetings’ programming delivered on its promises of “erratic coalitions” and produced a really enjoyable window into a scene that felt fresh in concert with its context. We began watching SUZY’s video loop Mezzo Forte. I’d arrived just before doors and was nestled in the back, sheltering from the already climbing heat. A montage of found footage, blurry, compressed, reeled around short spoken-word phrases and a set of ambient pads. I could maybe have been in a spa or an art installation - the eﬀect was a mixture of comfort and uncertainty. From where I was sitting the projection played partially through the punched metal railings around the venue’s recessed dancefloor. I could unfocus my eyes, which felt like the correct way to start a gig. Some people shuﬄed in, arranged themselves around the space, and settled in alongside me. The laptop screen playing the video was inverted, giving the impression that the video was being reflected from a body of very still water somewhere at chest height. I liked losing concentration as snippets of audio fell into place. “…organised by desire…”, “… to love one another…”. This was followed by the only act i was familiar with heading into the evening - a guitar performance by Christopher Jordan as Pentu. This felt colder than previous performances I’d seen by him; less Cantu-Ledesma or Fennesz and more Fripp/Eno. Notes of pedal steel and what I could only nail down as an “American” sound: plains and nighttime dust, mixed into a really beautiful guitar tone alongside added samples and distinctly digitised aesthetics. Pops, clicks, some synthesis on which to lay down slabs of soft metal. I wrote “Tone !!!” twice in my notes which I think gets to the core of why this performance worked so well. The swells of a slow attack pedal, the pseudo-dampness of a very cold concrete wall, and the compositional care of someone who is (rightly) starting to get booked more often in London. Take note. Mimiko followed, moving softly from tuning to playing. Accompanied by a second guitarist who harmonised, whistled, and chattered during the many breaks to re-tune. The music was quaint - slow waltzes and tender tunes in a distinctly eroded contemporary London style. Nestled between neofolk and neotwee you can find a huddle of  artists getting back to songwriting, and it was refreshing to tap directly into this vein and hear what someone has been making in their bedroom, unvarnished and bare. More widely this style can tend towards a totalising aesthetic and produce songs that are both deliberately unfinished and gratingly produced, but Mimiko trod a careful balance, weaving an incredibly-out-of-tune pair of guitars into a shy and dusty setlist. The evening ended on an “improvised trio” - Isaac Robertson on tenor sax, Anna Adetiba on alto, and Malachy O’Neill on drums. There’s a wider piece to be written about the growing prevalence of improvisation and free improvisation in London’s artschool-adjacent circles. See Grain and Life is Beautiful and Steam Down and countless others, stretched between experimental and jazz nodes. As creatively fulfilling as the act of improvising and learning to listen can be as a musician, the space aﬀorded also often leads to interstitial moments and an uneven experience as an audience: short loops, breaks, forced ambient sections as the group figures out what’s going on and where to go next. There were some of these moments, but the trio brought a structure to the set which forced a welcome forward momentum. O’Neill’s drums kept a consistency that let the saxophones range widely, while still playing into the reverb his kit was running through, and the trio tended towards a groove instead of wheeling out into space. Adetiba carried melodic tones on the alto, with Robertson playing rhythmically, getting the tenor down into gravel territory without overcooking it (sometimes I have horrifying flashbacks of tenor sax “subway battle” videos where a man in a snapback honks the shit out of a cover of Mister Saxobeat). They connected well together, the uncertain smiles which punctuated the finish refracting the event as a whole as the audience whistled and cheered. Smiles were shared. There’s much to be said about the collapse of music venues and musical cultures, but you can still find moments of intimacy just below the street’s surface. title: Republic of Ireland v Israel to be played at neutral venue - BBC
content: Dublin's Aviva Stadium was originally scheduled to host the fixture The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has confirmed the Republic of Ireland's home Nations League fixture with Israel later this year will take place at a neutral venue. The governing body's board has held meetings in recent weeks to discuss the "operational aspects" of hosting Israel at Dublin's Aviva Stadium on 4 October. On Friday, the FAI said Uefa approved a request to host the game at a neutral overseas venue and behind closed doors. The sides are also scheduled to meet at a neutral venue for Israel's home Group B3 match on 27 September. "Following consultation with various stakeholders, the Association is of the view that  operational challenges could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil, so the fixture will be played away from the Aviva Stadium," said the FAI. "The Association thanks An Garda Síochana [Irish police] for their support and advice over recent months and states that the decision to relocate to a neutral venue is one that has been considered an appropriate course of action by the FAI Board with the support of Uefa." Pressure has grown in Ireland for a boycott of the games because of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the Ireland Palestine Solidarity Campaign having held a protest at the Dáil (Irish parliament) last month. A 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport For Palestine, while May's 1-0 friendly victory over Qatar at Aviva Stadium was disrupted when tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on to the pitch. Following the Nations League draw in February, the FAI confirmed it would fulfil the fixtures, with chief executive David Courell saying the governing body had "no choice" and could face "serious consequences" if it pulled out of the games. Last month, experienced Republic of Ireland defender Seamus Coleman said the issue "should have been dealt with above us", while captain Nathan Collins said that if individual players felt strongly enough to boycott the games, "we are not going to stand against them". Players won't be stopped from taking stand - Collins on Israel fixtures 'We shouldn't be in this position' on Israel games - Coleman Last month, the Republic of Ireland's friendly with Qatar at Aviva Stadium was disrupted when tennis balls featuring the Palestinian flag were thrown on to the pitch On Friday, the FAI said it "understands and respects the views expressed by players and staff, supporters, its members, campaigners, members of the public and the Irish footballing community in relation to this fixture". The FAI also shared a statement from the Palestinian Football Association, which said: "The Palestinian Football Association expresses its appreciation for the principled positions taken by the Football Association of Ireland in support of the rights of the Palestinian people and Palestinian athletes. "The Palestinian Football Association also affirms its respect for the decision made by the Football Association of Ireland within the framework of its sporting and international obligations, in a manner that enables it to continue fulfilling its noble mission of serving football and promoting the values of justice, solidarity, and mutual respect." Despite having faced calls from within Ireland to boycott the games, the FAI insists it will fulfil the fixtures as pulling out of the matches would have "a profound impact on the whole of Irish football". It said the result of not fulfilling the games would be the forfeiture of six points which could lead to relegation to League C in the Nations League and an impact on the team's Uefa and Fifa rankings while highlighting that "the converse of these impacts would apply to Israel", increasing their chances of Nations League promotion and Euro 2028 qualification. "Beyond the sporting implications, there would be broader consequences for Irish football, such as reduced capacity to support clubs and leagues through critical services such as safeguarding, educational programmes, and player development opportunities," added the statement. "Also, the impact on Ireland international teams could result in the withdrawal of underage teams and a reduction in the level of support and services provided to players and staff." Last year, the FAI overwhelmingly approved a motion to call on Uefa to ban Israel from European club and international competitions. On Friday, the association said it "continues to reflect the sentiment" of that motion and said it will engage with its members at a forthcoming extraordinary general meeting. The Republic of Ireland will also face Austria and Kosovo in Group B3 of the 2026-27 Nations League. title: Greece Approves Acquisition of VICTA Diver Delivery Units and V-BAT Drones - navalnews.com
content: Home » Greece Approves Acquisition of VICTA Diver Delivery Units and V-BAT Drones The Parliament in Greece has approved more than €1 billion in defense procurements, including ten VICTA Diver Delivery Units from SubSea Craft and ten V-BAT reconnaissance VTOL drones from Shield AI. On June 11, 2026, the Special Permanent Committee on Armament Programs and Contracts of the Hellenic Parliament approved eight defense procurement programs worth more than €1 billion for the Hellenic Armed Forces. Among them is a program for the acquisition of ten VICTA Diver Delivery Units (DDUs) from the British SubSea Craft (SSC) and ten V-BAT reconnaissance Vertical Takeoff and Landing (VTOL) Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) from US company Shield AI. Regarding the V-BAT (designated as the MQ-35A), according to defencepoint.gr, six systems (12 aircraft and associated mission payloads) will be assigned to the Hellenic Army, while four systems (8 aircraft and associated mission payloads) will be delivered to the Hellenic Navy, with a two-year Follow-On Support (FOS) package included. The €71 million program will be implemented over a four-year period through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA). The V-BAT systems are already in service with the Hellenic Armed Forces. Two systems, comprising four aircraft, were acquired through a €5.75 million donation from shipowner Athanasios Laskaridis, with their official induction into service taking place on 14 May 2025. The V-BAT will provides tremendous intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting capabilities to the Hellenic Armed Forces. The acquisition of more platforms will increase Greece’s ability to maintain persistent maritime awareness and security in areas where traditional runway-dependent systems are harder to deploy and sustain. V-BAT is exceptionally well-suited for operations in Greece, where forces operate across dispersed islands, remote coastlines, deep valleys, mountain ranges, and complex maritime environments. V-BAT has proven itself in combat operations in Ukraine, including in GPS- and communications-denied environments, and was built for exactly these kinds of operational realities. We are proud to deepen our partnership with Greece and the Hellenic Armed Forces, The system has been already selected by the Navies of the United States, the Netherleands, Japan and Romania. Except for the V-BAT, the Hellenic Navy has recently contracted four Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 systems (each with two aircraft). These will equip the three Kimon-class frigates, along with the Navy’s training center in Marathon, although the system may be reassigned to other frigates if operational requirements change. According to G. Sideris of hellasjournal.com, there is also an intention to procure a fifth system in order to equip the fourth FDI HN frigate Themistocles (F-600) currently under construction. Regarding the VICTA DDU, the program is valued at €145 million. According to defencepoint.gr, six craft are intended for the Special Warfare Command (SWC) of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff (HNDGS), while four craft are designated for the Underwater Demolition Command (UDC) of the Hellenic Navy. The procurement package also includes Follow-On Support (FOS). VICTA combines the characteristics of a fast surface craft with those of a submersible. It is a next-generation maritime delivery platform capable of conducting high-speed surface transits before rapidly transitioning into a submerged, wet sub-surface mode for the covert insertion of personnel and equipment. This is  is enabled by an innovative fly-by-wire control system. While the baseline configuration is optimized for the clandestine delivery of special operations forces, its modular payload architecture allows the platform to be quickly reconfigured for a variety of mission profiles. A standardized rail system enables the carriage of operators, mission equipment, combat supplies, or specialized payloads, providing exceptional operational flexibility. Impressive performance on the surface (40kts and 250nm endurance) is matched by equally striking specification under water where 4hrs endurance is sufficient to navigate 2 crew and 6 divers for 25nm. Compatibility with a standard 40ft ISO shipping container makes it widely deployable. The platform can support a wide range of missions across the full spectrum of combat functions, including Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), fires, manoeuvre, force protection, command and control, and combat service support, delivering tactical effects in support of broader operational and strategic objectives. Naval News understands that the VICTA units for Greece will be constructed at the Skaramangas Shipyards under a partnership agreement with the manufacturer in Portsmouth, with more than 25 percent of the program’s value expected to be returned to the Greek industrial base. Furthermore, plans are reportedly being developed for the construction of an additional ten (10) VICTA systems in Greece for another NATO navy, potentially establishing Skaramangas as a regional production hub for the platform. volume 16,  Article number: 18277 (2026) Cite this article Clinical guidelines recommend a single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V) target of 1.2–1.4 per hemodialysis (HD) session, but optimal adequacy targets may differ by sex. We examined sex-specific associations between spKt/V and all-cause mortality in a nationwide Korean cohort of maintenance HD patients. Using data from the 2015 HD Quality Assessment and National Health Insurance Service, we included 29,349 adults on thrice-weekly HD. The association between spKt/V and mortality was estimated using Cox models, and Harrell’s C-index was used to derive sex-specific prognostic cut-off values. Of the cohort, 17,171 (58.5%) were men and 12,178 (41.5%) women, with mean follow-up 53.8 ± 23.0 months. The mean spKt/V was higher in women (1.71 ± 0.27) than in men (1.44 ± 0.22). In men, mortality was higher at spKt/V < 1.2 (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.14–1.37), with no additional benefit at 1.4 or higher. In women, survival improved in the higher categories (1.4–1.7: HR 0.86; ≥ 1.7: HR 0.73). C-index analysis identified a prognostic cutoff of 1.21 for men and 1.51 for women. These findings suggest that uniform adequacy thresholds may not fully reflect sex-related prognostic differences. The identified spKt/V values should be interpreted as data-driven prognostic reference points rather than prescriptive treatment targets, and warrant validation in prospective studies. Survival in patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) depends on the adequacy of hemodialysis (HD), which determines the efficiency of uremic toxin removal. Accurate identification and removal of uremic toxins, which vary significantly in size—from small molecules such as urea to larger ones like beta-2 microglobulin—is critical for effective dialysis management1. The dialysis dose, expressed as single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V), is the most widely used index for quantifying dialysis adequacy and predicting clinical outcomes2,3. Dialysis adequacy is typically assessed by measuring urea clearance using the Kt/V metric, which has contributed to the standardization of dialysis delivery and quality assessment worldwide1,4. Current clinical guidelines, including the Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI), recommend a spKt/V target of 1.4, with a minimum value of 1.2 per HD session for patients undergoing treatment three times per week5. However, these thresholds are largely derived from expert consensus and retrospective analyses rather than from large outcome-based studies6,7. The Hemodialysis (HEMO) study, the only large randomized trial evaluating dialysis dose, found no overall survival benefit with higher spKt/V levels8. Notably, sex-specific differences were observed: female patients in the high-dose dialysis group experienced a 19% reduced mortality risk compared to their counterparts in the standard-dose group, whereas male patients in the high-dose group exhibited a 16% increased mortality risk8. These findings highlight that the relationship between dialysis dose and patient survival may differ between men and women, suggesting potential limitations in relying solely on spKt/V as a universal marker of dialysis adequacy9. Additionally, spKt/V tends to overestimate dialysis adequacy in patients with smaller body sizes or malnutrition, as high spKt/V values might reflect reduced dialysis volume (V), indicative of decreased muscle mass or nutritional deficiencies10,11. Such overestimation may lead to premature session termination or reduced dialysis duration, potentially compromising long-term outcomes. Therefore, an individualized approach that considers sex, body composition, and clinical status is essential for accurately assessing dialysis adequacy. Despite these concerns, spKt/V remains the standard and widely accepted measure of dialysis adequacy. Regulatory standards, including those of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) in the United States and the Korean Hemodialysis Quality Assessment Program, require a minimum spKt/V of 1.2 for facility accreditation12,13,14. Yet, few studies have evaluated whether the optimal spKt/V thresholds differ by sex, and none have defined the quantitative cut-off values that minimize mortality risk in a large, ethnically homogeneous population. Given that Korean HD patients typically have smaller body size, longer treatment time, and highly standardized dialysis prescriptions due to a uniform reimbursement system, the nationwide Korean HD Quality Assessment dataset provides a unique opportunity to clarify these associations. Using this cohort, we aimed to determine the sex-specific optimal spKt/V thresholds associated with the lowest all-cause mortality and to assess whether higher dialysis dose confers differential survival benefits between men and women. Initially, 35,473 patients from 798 facilities were screened for eligibility. After excluding 5,601 patients (15.8%) with missing spKt/V values and 523 who underwent kidney transplantation before the index date, 29,349 patients were included in the final analysis (Supplementary Figure S1). The mean age of participants was 60.2 ± 12.8 years, with males comprising 58.5% of the study population. Diabetes was prevalent in 62.3% of patients, and the mean spKt/V was 1.55 ± 0.28 overall, 1.44 ± 0.22 for males, and 1.71 ± 0.27 for females. The overall proportion of patients with low dialysis adequacy (spKt/V < 1.2) was 7.3%, with a higher occurrence among males (10.6%) compared to females (1.7%) (Supplementary Table S1). When baseline characteristics were analyzed by sex (Table 1), both males and females showed significant differences across spKt/V categories. Among males, higher spKt/V values were associated with older age (P < 0.001), longer dialysis vintage (P < 0.001), and lower prevalence of diabetes mellitus (P < 0.001). Serum calcium levels increased (P < 0.001) and serum phosphorus levels decreased (P < 0.001) across higher spKt/V categories, whereas hemoglobin and albumin levels showed no significant variation. Among females, higher spKt/V was similarly associated with longer dialysis vintage (P < 0.001) and lower body mass index (P < 0.001), accompanied by higher calcium (P < 0.001) and lower phosphorus concentrations (P < 0.001). Blood pressure tended to decrease with increasing spKt/V in both sexes (P < 0.001). SpKt/V values demonstrated a significant negative correlation with body weight. Notably, this inverse relationship was stronger among male patients than female patients (P < 0.001). Across the entire spectrum of patient weights, females consistently exhibited higher mean spKt/V values compared to males (Supplementary Figure S2). Over a mean follow-up duration of 53.8 ± 23.0 months, there were 10,453 deaths, yielding a crude mortality rate of 79.5 per 1,000 person-years (Supplementary Table S2). In male patients (Table 2A), a total of 6,414 deaths were recorded over 75,597 person-years, corresponding to a crude mortality rate of 84.8 per 1,000 person-years. The lowest mortality rate was observed in the spKt/V 1.2–1.4 group (78.7 per 1,000 person-years), while mortality increased at both lower (< 1.2) and higher (≥ 1.7) spKt/V categories, reaching 94.1 per 1,000 person-years in the highest group. In female patients (Table 2B), 4,039 deaths occurred during 55,926 person-years, yielding a crude mortality rate of 72.2 per 1,000 person-years. Mortality rates gradually decreased with increasing spKt/V, from 88.8 per 1,000 person-years in the < 1.2 group to 67.8 per 1,000 person-years in those with spKt/V ≥ 1.7. Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated the lowest mortality for males at spKt/V values of 1.2–1.4 and significantly improved survival for females at spKt/V levels of 1.4–1.7 and  ≥ 1.7 (Fig. 1A and B). Kaplan-Meier survival curves according to categorical single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V). Differences in survival among groups were assessed using the log-rank test. (A) Survival curves for male patients categorized into four groups based on spKt/V values: <1.2, 1.2–1.4, 1.4–1.7, and ≥ 1.7. Highest survival rates were observed in males with spKt/V values of 1.2–1.4. (B) Survival curves for female patients categorized into four groups based on spKt/V values: <1.2, 1.2–1.4, 1.4–1.7, and ≥ 1.7. Females with higher spKt/V values (> 1.4) exhibited significantly improved survival compared to those with lower spKt/V (< 1.4). * P value < 0.05. The discriminative performance of spKt/V for all-cause mortality was evaluated using Harrell’s C-index across 0.01-unit increments. In the overall cohort, the C-index peaked at spKt/V 1.32, indicating the optimal threshold for mortality prediction (Fig. 2A). When stratified by sex, the C-index showed distinct patterns: the maximum value occurred at 1.21 in males (Fig. 2B) and 1.51 in females (Fig. 2C), identifying the sex-specific optimal spKt/V cutoffs associated with the lowest mortality risk. Beyond these values, the C-index plateaued or declined slightly, suggesting no further improvement in predictive accuracy. C-index curves for predicting all-cause mortality according to single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V). C-index values were calculated across 0.01-unit increments of spKt/V. The red dotted lines indicate the spKt/V value corresponding to the maximum C-index. (A) Total population: The highest C-index (0.7283) was observed at a spKt/V of 1.32. (B) Male patients: The maximum C-index (0.7227) was observed at a spKt/V of 1.21. (C) Female patients: The maximum C-index (0.7361) was observed at a spKt/V of 1.51. Beyond these values, the C-index plateaued or declined slightly, suggesting no further improvement in predictive accuracy. Cox proportional hazards analysis demonstrated significant sex-specific differences in the relationship between spKt/V and all-cause mortality. For males, univariate analysis indicated increased mortality risk at spKt/V ≥ 1.4 (1.4–1.7, hazard ratio (HR) 1.12, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.06–1.18, P < 0.001; ≥ 1.7, HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.10–1.31, P < 0.001) compared to the reference range (spKt/V 1.2–1.4). However, multivariate adjustment demonstrated significantly elevated mortality risk only for spKt/V < 1.2 (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.14–1.37), with no additional benefit for spKt/V ≥ 1.4 (Table 3). In contrast, females exhibited reduced mortality risk at higher spKt/V levels in both univariate and multivariate analyses. Specifically, spKt/V values of 1.4–1.7 and ≥ 1.7 were significantly associated with lower mortality (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.96, P = 0.008 and HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65–0.82, P < 0.001, respectively), whereas spKt/V < 1.2 showed no significant mortality impact (Table 4). In fully adjusted models treating spKt/V as a continuous variable, higher spKt/V was consistently associated with lower mortality risk in both sexes, with the protective effect being stronger for females (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.58–0.74; P < 0.001) compared to males (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70–0.90; P < 0.001) (Supplementary Table S3). Figure 3 presents the adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality according to spKt/V categories in males and females. In males, mortality risk increased markedly when spKt/V was below 1.2, with the lowest adjusted risk observed in the 1.2–1.4 range (Fig. 3A). Beyond this level, hazard ratios remained stable, indicating a plateau of survival benefit. In females, mortality risk decreased progressively with higher spKt/V values, showing a stepwise decline across 1.2–1.4, 1.4–1.7, and ≥ 1.7 categories (Fig. 3B). The lowest adjusted hazard was observed at spKt/V ≥ 1.7. The vertical dashed lines in both panels represent the spKt/V thresholds identified by Harrell’s C-index analysis (1.21 for males and 1.51 for females), which correspond closely to the observed points of minimal mortality risk. Adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality according to single-pool Kt/V (spKt/V) categories. Multivariate Cox regression models were constructed to assess the association between spKt/V and mortality. The spKt/V threshold associated with the highest Harrell’s C-index for mortality discrimination is indicated. Multivariate Model 1 included adjusted age, dialysis vintage, and body mass index; Model 2 was further adjusted for medical comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular accident, and atrial fibrillation); Model 3 (full model) included all previous variables with additionally included clinical laboratory parameters (plasma hemoglobin, serum albumin, calcium, phosphorus). (A) In males, mortality risk rose sharply below spKt/V 1.21, with the lowest risk observed in the 1.2–1.4 range. Further increases in spKt/V above this range showed limited additional survival benefit. (B) In females, mortality risk progressively decreased with spKt/V above 1.51, showing significant reductions in the 1.4–1.7, and ≥ 1.7 categories compared with lower ranges. In this large national cohort of Korean HD patients, higher spKt/V was associated with lower all-cause mortality, but the strength and threshold of this relationship differed markedly by sex. Using Harrell’s C-index, the spKt/V values associated with the lowest mortality risk were identified as 1.21 for males and 1.51 for females, and these thresholds corresponded closely with the nadir of the adjusted hazard ratio curves. Specifically, mortality was significantly lower in females at spKt/V levels ≥ 1.4, whereas in males, no additional survival benefit was observed beyond a spKt/V of 1.2–1.4. These findings suggest that dialysis adequacy assessment may require consideration of sex-based physiological differences. An unexpected finding was the absence of additional survival benefit and a slight increase in mortality risk among males in the higher spKt/V categories. This observation may reflect reverse causation, as patients with greater illness severity or inflammatory burden may have received intensified dialysis prescriptions despite poorer baseline health status7. In addition, higher spKt/V in males may partly represent reduced body mass or sarcopenia rather than true dialysis intensification, which has been associated with adverse outcomes in dialysis populations15. Residual confounding related to unmeasured factors such as nutritional status, frailty, or dialysis prescription characteristics (e.g., treatment time or blood flow rate) cannot be excluded. Importantly, higher spKt/V may in some patients reflect adverse clinical states rather than greater effective dialysis delivery itself. Accordingly, the observed association should be interpreted cautiously, particularly when considering causal implications, and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of harm from higher dialysis dose itself8. The HEMO study, the only large randomized controlled trial investigating dialysis dose, found no overall benefit of increased dialysis dose regarding survival, hospitalization rates, or serum albumin levels8. Interestingly, gender-specific results emerged, with females in the high-dose group experiencing a 19% reduction in mortality risk compared to the standard-dose group, whereas males exhibited a 16% increase in mortality risk8. These gender-specific outcomes from the HEMO study suggest limitations in relying solely on spKt/V to assess dialysis adequacy and emphasize the importance of sex-related biological factors9. Similar results have been reported from international cohorts. The DOPPS analysis by Hecking et al. showed that women start dialysis later, receive higher spKt/V, yet lose their natural survival advantage compared with men, indicating that “equal dose” may translate into “relative underdialysis” for females16. Likewise, a large multicenter European study from DaVita clinics demonstrated consistently higher spKt/V values in women despite equal treatment time, highlighting that spKt/V may overestimate dialysis adequacy in smaller body sizes17. Consistent with previous studies, our analysis showed an inverse relationship between body weight and spKt/V, which was more pronounced in males18,19. The proportion of males with inadequate dialysis (spKt/V < 1.2) was substantially higher (10.6%) compared to females (1.7%). Cox proportional hazards analyses indicated that males with spKt/V < 1.2 had a 25% higher mortality risk compared to those within the optimal spKt/V range of 1.2–1.4, while higher spKt/V values provided no further benefit. Conversely, females demonstrated a significant survival advantage at spKt/V levels ≥ 1.4, with a mortality reduction of up to 27% at spKt/V ≥ 1.7. These findings corroborate previous studies suggesting stronger associations between spKt/V and mortality in females18,20. The inverse association between body weight and spKt/V can be partly explained by the mathematical structure of the spKt/V formula, in which the urea distribution volume (V) increases with greater body mass9,21. As a result, individuals with larger body size—particularly males, who generally have higher muscle mass and total body water—may exhibit lower calculated spKt/V values even when receiving comparable dialysis prescriptions15. In addition, sex-related differences in body composition and surface area–to–volume ratios may further accentuate this pattern. These considerations suggest that variations in spKt/V by body weight do not necessarily reflect differences in dialysis delivery alone but also underlying anthropometric characteristics. The observed sex differences in spKt/V thresholds may be explained by physiological variations. Ramirez et al. suggested that adjusting dialysis dose calculations from a volume-based spKt/V to a body surface area (BSA)-based spKt/V could clarify the relationship between dialysis dose and mortality9. The glomerular filtration rate, inherently proportional to BSA, tends to be similar in adult males and females with equivalent BSA levels22. However, males typically exhibit a 12–15% higher ratio of volume (V) to BSA compared to females, suggesting that BSA-normalized spKt/V may better reflect dialysis adequacy than volume-normalized spKt/V9. These physiologic differences may partly explain why higher spKt/V ranges were associated with lower mortality in women9,20. Currently, spKt/V remains the most widely used measure of dialysis adequacy, and clinical guidelines recommend a minimum target of 1.25. Our results indicate that while this threshold is appropriate for men, it may be insufficient for women. The spKt/V values identified in this study (1.21 for men and 1.51 for women) may have implications for dialysis risk stratification and quality assessment. Most dialysis facilities currently apply uniform prescriptions regardless of sex, guided by a spKt/V benchmark in reimbursement and quality assessment programs. However, our data indicate that such a one-size-fits-all approach may lead to relative underdialysis in women. Implementing sex-specific adequacy targets, or at least recognizing physiological differences in dose requirements, could help improve dialysis equity and patient survival. Future clinical research should evaluate whether applying these differentiated targets can translate into measurable survival benefits. Importantly, the sex-specific spKt/V values identified in this study were derived from a prognostic, data-driven approach using Harrell’s C-index and therefore should be interpreted as reference thresholds associated with mortality risk rather than prescriptive treatment targets. These thresholds are intended primarily as markers for prognostic risk stratification and hypothesis generation rather than direct targets for prescription adjustment. Prospective and interventional studies incorporating detailed anthropometric and dialysis prescription parameters are required before these observations can be translated into formal guideline recommendations. This study’s strengths include its large-scale, nationally representative sample from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA), enabling extensive follow-up and robust data analysis. However, several limitations should be noted. First, only spKt/V was evaluated, and BSA-normalized Kt/V was not considered because the national database did not provide sufficient anthropometric and session-specific prescription variables to allow reliable calculation of BSA-adjusted indices. Future studies incorporating detailed height, post-dialysis weight, and treatment parameters may further clarify whether BSA-normalized dose metrics refine sex-specific prognostic thresholds. Second, the specific causes of death and disease-specific mortality were not analyzed. Third, although major cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities were adjusted for, residual confounding from unmeasured or incompletely coded clinical conditions—including differences in body composition, nutritional status, frailty, and dialysis prescription characteristics such as treatment time or blood flow rate—cannot be entirely excluded. In particular, higher spKt/V may partly reflect lower body mass, sarcopenia, or frailty rather than greater effective dialysis delivery, which limits causal interpretation of the observed associations. Lastly, due to the observational nature of the study, causality cannot be definitively established, and whether adjusting dialysis prescriptions would enhance outcomes remains unclear. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that optimal dialysis dosing differs by biological sex: men were associated with the lowest mortality within the spKt/V range of 1.2–1.4, whereas women were associated with lower mortality at higher spKt/V values. Recognition of these sex-specific differences may help contextualize dialysis adequacy assessment and support future prospective studies evaluating individualized dosing strategies. This longitudinal observational cohort study included Korean patients undergoing maintenance HD. Data from the 2015 Hemodialysis Quality Assessment conducted by the HIRA were utilized, and mortality data were collected from January 2016 through November 2021. The HIRA database includes tertiary hospitals, general hospitals, and private dialysis clinics across all regions of Korea, ensuring national representativeness. Patients who underwent kidney transplantation prior to the assessment date, those hospitalized, or patients lost to follow-up during the assessment period were excluded from analysis13. HD quality assessment data were collected via a standardized web-based system implemented in each dialysis facility, capturing 12 key measures across three domains: structure, process, and outcome. Data accuracy was validated through periodic audits by HIRA to ensure data completeness and reliability. Patient demographic factors, including age, sex, dialysis duration, body mass index (BMI), and health insurance status, were retrieved from the HIRA database. Comorbid conditions, such as diabetes mellitus (ICD-10: E10–E14), hypertension (I10–I13, I15), ischemic heart disease (I20–I25), congestive heart failure (I50), atrial fibrillation (I48), and cerebrovascular disease (I60–I64, I69), were identified through ICD-10 codes documented in claims data from January to December 2015. Pre-dialysis systolic and diastolic blood pressure were also recorded. Laboratory parameters, including plasma hemoglobin, serum albumin, calcium, and phosphorus, were measured monthly, and the mean of three measurements was used for analysis. Dialysis adequacy was evaluated using the spKt/V. Dialysis adequacy was evaluated quarterly by measuring spKt/V or urea reduction ratio (URR). Facilities reported the proportion of patients achieving a spKt/V ≥ 1.2 or URR ≥ 65%, which contributed to their HD facility star ratings. The spKt/V was calculated using Daugirdas’ second-generation formula: Kt/V = -ln (R − 0.008 × t) + (4–3.5 × R) × UF/W, where UF is ultrafiltration volume (liters), W is post-dialysis weight (kg), and R is the ratio of post- to pre-dialysis blood urea nitrogen levels21. The primary outcome measure was all-cause mortality. Mortality was ascertained by linking the HIRA claims database with the official national death registry provided by Statistics Korea, which contains legally registered death records23. Patients who received kidney transplant during the follow-up period were censored at the time of kidney transplantation. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Hallym University Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital (No. HKS 2021-11-043) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The IRB waived the requirement for written informed consent due to the retrospective nature of the study and because participants were anonymized. Patients were categorized into four groups based on baseline spKt/V: <1.2, 1.2–1.4, 1.4–1.7, and ≥ 1.7. Continuous variables were summarized as means ± standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, as appropriate, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Group comparisons were performed using the independent t-test or one-way analysis of variance for normally distributed variables and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test or Kruskal–Wallis test for non-normally distributed variables. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Survival analyses utilized Kaplan-Meier methods, with differences between groups evaluated by the log-rank test. Two-sided p values were reported throughout, with statistical significance defined as p < 0.05. Cox proportional hazards models were performed to assess the independent relationship between spKt/V and mortality. Three models were constructed: Model 1 adjusted for age, sex, dialysis vintage, and BMI; Model 2 was further adjusted for medical comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular accident, and atrial fibrillation). These comorbidities were selected a priori because they represent standard and widely used prognostic variables in mortality analyses of maintenance hemodialysis populations. Additional clinical conditions were reviewed but were not included if their coding reliability or prevalence was insufficient to ensure model stability; Model 3 additionally included clinical laboratory parameters (plasma hemoglobin, serum albumin, calcium, phosphorus). To identify the sex-specific optimal spKt/V thresholds, we calculated Harrell’s C-index for mortality prediction across 0.01-unit increments of spKt/V. Harrell’s C-index was selected because it evaluates the discriminative performance of continuous predictors in survival data without assuming predefined thresholds. The value yielding the highest C-index was considered the optimal cutoff. Model performance was compared using changes in C-index values, and proportional hazards assumptions were verified using Schoenfeld residuals. The continuous association between spKt/V and mortality risk was also examined using restricted cubic spline functions. Assessment of distributional assumptions using the Shapiro–Wilk test indicated that several continuous laboratory variables deviated from normality, whereas age and dialysis vintage approximated a normal distribution. Accordingly, both parametric and non-parametric statistical tests were applied depending on variable characteristics. All analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.3; R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Statistical significance was defined as a p < 0.05. title: Waynedale's assertiveness leads to Div. V state semifinal win - Wooster Daily Record
content: CANTON — Down one run in the third inning of the Division V state semifinal game in Canton at Thurman Munson Memorial Stadium on Thursday afternoon and after seeing Lucasville Valley starting pitcher Nolan Barnett once already, Waynedale's lineup was about to get in sync. Waynedale's (29-3) assertiveness and readiness worked in their favor, as the Golden Bears — in their fifth straight state semifinal appearance — defeated Lucasville Valley (22-8), 7-2. With that, the defending Division V state champions will play Gahanna Columbus Academy Friday, June 12 in Akron for a chance at not just repeating but winning four state titles in five years. "Our team 1 through 9 have great hitters and we adjust really well to pitchers," said Waynedale left fielder Cam Miller afterwards. "We kind of knew his stuff and we prepared for it all week." Miller scored the first run of the game in the first inning after being driven in by starting pitcher Jordan Miller. Cam Miller's opposite field RBI double then tied things up at 2-2. Centerfielder Hudson Barkman delivered on an RBI single to give the Golden Bears the lead. That third inning was the turning point for Waynedale, as their depth and ability to use all parts of the field paved the way. "We call it a three-quarters arm slot pitcher. We watched video of him, so we knew what it was going to look like," said Waynedale head coach Lucas Daugherty. "... After we saw him through the lineup, we were able to lay off the stuff from the bottom of the zone and the balls that drops out. That's what he does well. Everything sinks. Once we were able to lay off the ones low and make him bring it up again, it really gave us a chance." Cam Miller, who went 4-for-4 with four hits, 2 RBIs and scored three runs in the game, said the pitch he and his teammates saw the best from Barnett was his fastball. "Up to that point, I was seeing the ball great. I took whatever he gave me," he said. Waynedale eventually outhit Lucasville Valley 13-5, with Jordan Miller — who also earned the win as the starting pitcher — driving in two runs and Barkman adding three RBIs. If the little things are important come playoff baseball, it's running the bases through and through, which Waynedale did with intent. There were a couple of times when the Indians infield wasn't able to field a ground ball cleanly and players such as Brayden Steiner, Maddox Kidd and Collin McGlothlin ran down the first base line and ended up safe. Those basic plays helped the Golden Bears extend some innings that eventually led to more runs being scored. "We always try to put pressure there. We run hard," said Cam, who entered the game in the bottom of the sixth inning and had a key bases loaded, two-out strikeout to get Waynedale out of trouble. "That's really an expectation there," Daugherty said. "We tell the guys, leave it all out there. Whether you're popping the ball in the air or on the ground weak, run it out. Put pressure on them and make them make plays. That probably helped us add a couple of more runs in the game." "We're definitely gonna let this win sink in but we're not down yet," Cam said. "We're hungry for more. We're not satisfied with winning one game. We want to win it all."

title: Supreme Court Unanimously Upholds SEC Disgorgement Powers in Sripetch v. SEC - Foley & Lardner LLP
content: Foley Achieves Top Rankings in Chambers USA 2026: Discover What Sets Us Apart Innovation in Energy & Infrastructure Aviation & Aircraft Transactions Regulatory Compliance, Food Safety Infringement Litigation, Leasing Advances in Health Care & Life Sciences Banking & Finance, Cannabis Litigation Hotels & Resorts, Golf Clubs Sports Facility Development, Media Deals Leveraging AI, Cloud Computing, Genomics Generational Wealth, Wealth Management Offshore Oil & Gas, Admiralty Law End-to-End Business Solutions Trademark, Manufacturing, Supply Chain Public Affairs, Small Business Services On June 4, 2026, the United States Supreme Court handed down a 9-0 decision in Sripetch v. Securities and Exchange Commission, No. 25-466, affirming that proof of pecuniary loss to victims of securities law violations is not a prerequisite for the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to secure a disgorgement remedy.[1] This is the only clear holding of the opinion, which left open several questions surrounding the SEC’s disgorgement remedy. Justice Neil Gorsuch authored the majority opinion, which resolves a circuit split in which the First and Ninth Circuits had permitted disgorgement without a showing of investor losses, while the Second Circuit required such a showing.[2] The decision declined to require this additional showing which could have restricted the SEC’s ability to obtain disgorgement in insider trading and other cases where losses could not be attributed directly to harmed victims. The underlying dispute traces back to a series of securities fraud schemes orchestrated by Ongkaruck Sripetch, who manipulated the share prices of more than 20 penny-stock companies through pump and dump tactics. The SEC filed a civil enforcement action, and Sripetch ultimately consented to have judgment entered against him. However, he later challenged the Commission’s effort to recover more than $4.1 million in disgorgement, contending that it was impermissible under Liu v. SEC, 591 U.S. 71 (2020), absent evidence that his conduct actually caused monetary harm to investors since under that case disgorged funds must be awarded for victims. The Ninth Circuit ruled against Sripetch, concluding that demonstrating pecuniary loss to investors is unnecessary to support a disgorgement order. That ruling widened an existing divide among the appellate courts: the First and Ninth Circuits had aligned with the SEC’s position, while the Second Circuit reached the contrary conclusion. The Supreme Court took up the case to resolve this conflict. Justice Gorsuch anchored the Court’s reasoning in longstanding principles of equity. The opinion drew a distinction between legal damages for losses and equitable recovery of profits that deprived wrongdoers of unlawful activity. The opinion explains that under equitable principles a plaintiff need not demonstrate any resulting financial losses. Rather, it is sufficient that the claimant’s legally protected interests were invaded — even if that invasion produced no quantifiable monetary harm. Relying on these equitable principles, the Court held that proof of investor loss was not required for the SEC to obtain disgorgement. In its holding, the Court dodged what appeared to be a relevant issue in the case. That issue is the scope of the SEC’s disgorgement authority under §78u(d)(5) as compared to such authority under §78u(d)(7).[3] Under §78u(d)(5), the SEC traditionally sought disgorgement under equitable principles subject to the associated legal limitations. The SEC’s authority under this provision had been limited by Liu. Under §78u(d)(7), sometimes referred to as the “Liu fix”, the SEC argued Congress gave it the authority to seek disgorgement in any case where a defendant was unjustly enriched regardless of equitable considerations. The Court declined to reconcile the two statutory provisions, content to resolve the narrow issue of whether proof of investor losses is required (under either provision) for the SEC to receive a disgorgement award. The Court also rejected arguments raised by Sripetch. First, the Court rejected the argument that Liu foreclosed the result since, according to that case, disgorgement must be “awarded for victims.” The Court reasoned that equitable principles allowed for victims without actual losses so long as legally protected interests were violated. Next, the Court dismissed Sripetch’s arguments that the SEC could in the future sidestep equity altogether by pursuing disgorgement solely under §78u(d)(7) based on unjust enrichment and not “award” disgorgement for victims at all and instead pay disgorgement to the U.S. Treasury. Again, the Court declined to reconcile the two statutory provisions, instead sticking to the narrow question of whether proof of investor losses is required under either provision. However, the Court appeared to suggest that disgorgement under §78u(d)(7) could be subject to the equitable constraints under Liu and now Sripetch which could be read as a shot across the SEC’s bow. Justice Thomas joined the result but penned a separate concurrence raising a question he believes the Court must soon confront: whether post-Liu statutory changes under §78u(d)(7) have transformed disgorgement into a legal remedy that entitles defendants to a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment. In his view, Congress’s decision to carve disgorgement out of the general equitable-relief provision and assign it a distinct limitations period signals a legislative intent to treat it as a legal, rather than equitable, remedy. Justice Thomas further observed that the SEC’s enforcement record is difficult to square with equitable principles, pointing out that in fiscal year 2024 the agency secured $6.1 billion in disgorgement but distributed only $345 million back to investors — a disparity he likened to a penalty system rather than a compensatory one. This issue appears to be somewhat academic, as the SEC normally seeks civil penalties in cases where it is seeking disgorgement. As such, based on the civil penalty remedy, defendants already have a right to jury trial in most, if not all cases that include a disgorgement remedy.[4] We suspect the SEC would readily trade a jury trial right for recognition that disgorgement is a stand-alone legal remedy unmoored from equitable principles. The ruling represents a meaningful but mixed win for the Commission. SEC General Counsel Russell McGranahan praised the outcome, emphasizing its importance for enforcement consistency and the agency’s broader anti-fraud agenda.[5] No doubt the practical implications are significant. Entities and individuals facing SEC enforcement actions cannot defeat disgorgement by arguing that the agency failed to identify investors who lost money. Instead, the SEC need only show that the defendant’s conduct invaded investors’ legally protected interests. On the other hand, the Court’s failure to reconcile the two statutory provisions under §78u(d)(5) and §78u(d)(7) should be concerning to the SEC. The Court certainly did not view the latter provision as being the “Liu fix” as the SEC had hoped. Going forward, questions remain about the SEC’s authority to seek disgorgement in cases where funds will be paid to the U.S. Treasury and not to victims of securities law violations. This impacts insider trading cases, where victims normally cannot be identified. It’s unclear whether the SEC would be permitted to demonstrate infeasibility in providing funds to victims in this context in order to remit disgorgement to the U.S. Treasury, and what showing would be required to do so. Given the narrow holding of the Sripetch decision and the many questions it left unresolved, there is no doubt the scope of the SEC’s disgorgement remedy will continue to be litigated in the appellate courts particularly in insider trading cases and other cases where funds are going to the U.S. Treasury and not victims. At the end of the day, the only clear takeaway from the Sripetch decision is that proof of investor loss is not required for an award of disgorgement. title: Coe v. Blanche - American Civil Liberties Union
content: With immigrant rights, trans justice, reproductive freedom, and more at risk, we’re in courts and communities across the country to protect everyone’s rights — and we need you with us. Your contribution to the ACLU will ensure we have the resources to protect people's rights and defend our democracy. Thanks for your support! Three New York families with adolescent transgender children and two transgender New Yorkers filed a class action lawsuit to protect patient identifying and sensitive health information from being turned over to the Department of Justice in response to federal grand jury subpoenas issued as part of a widespread effort to "end” necessary health care for transgender adolescents. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. In May 2026, NYU Langone Hospitals received a grand jury subpoena signed by an Assistant U.S. Attorney located in Fort Worth, Texas, which demanded that they turn over the identities and medical records of any patient who had received medical treatment for gender dysphoria while they were under 18 years old from NYU Langone, from January 2020 through May 2026. Other healthcare institutions in New York City, including Mount Sinai Health System, may have received similar or identical subpoenas. The grand jury subpoenas followed a year-long effort by the Department of Justice to obtain private medical records through administrative subpoenas—efforts that were repeatedly blocked by at least eight federal district court judges. One court dismissed the government’s reasoning as a “smokescreen,” while another concluded the DOJ “issued the subpoena first and searched for a justification second.” In June 2026, a lawsuit was filed in the Southern District of New York by the American Civil Liberties Union, the New York Civil Liberties Union, and Lambda Legal on behalf of three families with transgender youth and two transgender adults who were minors when they began care. It requests a temporary restraining order blocking the subpoenas from being enforced against NYU Langone, Mt. Sinai, their affiliated providers, as well as any other New York City provider of gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. All plaintiffs have filed under pseudonyms to maintain their privacy and anonymity. The lawsuit covers “all individuals who received any medical treatment for gender dysphoria, … while they were under eighteen years of age, from January 1, 2020, through May 5, 2026, at a healthcare institution located in New York City, including NYU Langone Hospitals (and any other NYU entity) and Mount Sinai Health System.” The plaintiffs charge the Department of Justice with violating their Fourth and Fifth Amendment privacy and due process rights. The plaintiffs also sue NYU Langone to prevent its release of information protected by doctor-patient privilege under New York state law.

title: EPA Restores Title V Affirmative Defense Protections - Mayer Brown
content: On  June 1, 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) issued a final rule withdrawing a 2023 rule, Removal  of Title V Emergency Affirmative Defense Provisions From State Operating Permit  Programs and Federal Operating Permit Program (the “2023 Affirmative  Defense Rule”). The withdrawal reinstates the longstanding emergency-related  affirmative defense provisions in the EPA’s Title V operating permit program  that shield regulated entities against claims for noncompliance with  technology-based emission limitations during an emergency. Title  V of the Clean Air Act (“CAA”), enacted in 1990, establishes a permitting  regime for facilities that emit air pollution.1 Under this framework, all operators  of stationary sources of air pollution are required to apply for and hold a  Title V permit, which must list the “enforceable emission limitations and  standards” applicable to the source under the CAA.2 If an operator violates  the emission limitations and standards incorporated in its permit, the operator  can be sued for injunctive relief and “any appropriate civil penalties.”3 Subsequent regulations,  however, created “an affirmative defense to an action brought for noncompliance  with . . . technology-based emission limitations” during an emergency.4 Those provisions had  defined an “emergency” as “any situation arising from sudden and reasonably  unforeseeable events beyond the control of the source, including acts of God,  which situation requires immediate corrective action to restore normal  operation, and that causes the source to exceed a technology-based emission  limitation under the permit, due to unavoidable increases in emissions  attributable to the emergency.”5 On  July 21, 2023, the EPA issued the 2023 Affirmative Defense Rule, which  rescinded the emergency-related affirmative defense provisions based on the EPA’s  conclusion that they were legally impermissible under the CAA.6 As a consequence, states  were likewise required to remove from their operating permit program  regulations and existing operating permits any State affirmative defense  provisions based on the rescinded Federal provisions.7 SSM  Litigation Group filed a petition for review of the 2023 Affirmative Defense  Rule in the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit. On September 5, 2025, the  court issued its decision in SSM Litig. Grp. v. EPA, 150 F.4th 593 (D.C.  Cir. 2025), finding that the EPA’s 2023 Affirmative Defense Rule was “unreasonable  and not in accordance with law” and rested “entirely on erroneous legal  justifications.”8 The court issued its mandate on January 12, 2026, after denying a petition for  rehearing on January 2, 2026. Following  the DC Circuit’s decision, the EPA has now formally withdrawn the 2023  Affirmative Defense Rule. The effect of this final action is to restore the  text of 40 CFR 70.6(g) and 71.6(g) as those provisions existed before the 2023  rule—that is, to reinstate the emergency-related affirmative defense provisions  in their entirety. The  EPA issued this action as a final rule without notice-and-comment rulemaking,  invoking the Administrative Procedure Act’s “good cause” exemption under 5  U.S.C. 553(b)(B). The Agency determined that providing a public hearing or an  opportunity for comment was unnecessary because the withdrawal is a “ministerial  act necessary to carry out the D.C. Circuit’s mandate” involving “no exercise  of Agency discretion.” For the same reasons, the EPA invoked good cause under 5  U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to make the rule effective immediately upon publication in the  Federal Register. The  EPA also characterized this action as an Executive Order 14192 deregulatory  action,9 noting that it provides  burden reduction because State, local, and Tribal permitting authorities are no  longer required to submit revisions to their Title V operating permit programs  or to revise existing operating permits. With  the withdrawal now effective, the emergency affirmative defense at 40 CFR  70.6(g) and 71.6(g) is once again available to permittees. Under the reinstated  provisions, a permittee may assert the affirmative defense in an enforcement  proceeding for noncompliance with technology-based emission limitations if it  demonstrates through properly signed, contemporaneous operating logs or other  relevant evidence that: The  permittee bears the burden of proof in establishing the occurrence of an  emergency. Importantly, the definition of “emergency” does not include  noncompliance caused by improperly designed equipment, lack of preventive  maintenance, careless or improper operation, or operator error. This  withdrawal carries several implications for regulated entities and State  permitting authorities: State  and local program revisions are no longer required. State, local, and Tribal  permitting authorities are no longer required to submit revisions to their Title  V operating permit programs or to revise existing operating permits to  implement the requirements of the now-withdrawn 2023 rule. Jurisdictions that  had already removed or modified their emergency affirmative defense provisions  to comply with the 2023 rule will consider reinstating them. Affirmative  defense is available again. Owners and operators of sources holding Title V operating permits once again  have access to the emergency affirmative defense for exceedances of  technology-based emission limitations resulting from qualifying emergencies.  This restoration of the regulatory status quo provides significant operational  certainty for facilities that may experience sudden, unforeseeable disruptions. Documentation  is critical. Because the affirmative defense must be demonstrated through properly signed,  contemporaneous operating logs or other relevant evidence, facilities should  ensure that their emergency response protocols include real-time documentation  of emergency events, the actions taken to minimize excess emissions, and timely  notification to the permitting authority. The  EPA’s withdrawal of the 2023 Affirmative Defense Rule marks a return to the  longstanding regulatory framework under which permittees may assert an  emergency affirmative defense against enforcement actions for exceedances of  technology-based emission limitations. Regulated entities should review their  operating procedures to ensure they are positioned to take advantage of the  reinstated provisions, with particular attention to contemporaneous  documentation and timely notification requirements. Mayer Brown will continue  to monitor developments in this space, including any potential challenges to  the withdrawal itself. 6 Removal  of Title V Emergency Affirmative Defense Provisions From State Operating Permit  Programs and Federal Operating Permit Program, 88 Fed. Reg. 47,029 (July 21,  2023). 8 SSM  Litig. Grp. v. Env’t Prot. Agency,  150 F.4th 593, 599-600 (D.C. Cir. 2025). 9“ Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” Exec. Order No. 14192, 90  FR 9065 (Jan. 31, 2025). 10 40  C.F.R. § 70.6(g)(3); 40 C.F.R. § 71.6(g)(3). title: USA v. Germany, 2026 Friendly; What we Learned - Stars and Stripes FC
content: The scoreline might have gone Germany’s way, but there was a lot to be optimistic with the United States Mens National Teams performance in their 2-1 loss. Despite not winning the game, the US showed a lot of good moments against Germany, holding a lot of possession, winning the ball back aggressively and up the field, limiting Germany’s chances, and creating their own moments at goal. But it was the kind of performance where it is really kinda hard to talk about anything concrete. It was more a vibe test, a check to see if the US is at the level that they need to be going into the World Cup. And it’s not just me saying that. After the game, Tyler Adams said exactly that: I don’t think any of these tune up games are about tactics, do you know what I mean? Like, we’ve trained together, we’ve played together, we’ve worked under Mauricio for a year and a half now. Like we understand the tactics. It has to be about the mentality and if we are ready for the moment. And I think today we showed we are ready for the moment. - Tyler Adams Add Stars and Stripes FC as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. I have to agree with Adams here. This was a game about showing up and being present and competing. And the US very much did that. That said, there is one thing that I wanted to talk about. I think it is pretty clear that we should expect the lineup from this game to be what we see against Paraguay with only a few wrinkles. That lineup looks something like this Matt Freese (goalkeeper)Alex Freeman (Centerback) Miles Robinson Chris Richards (Centerback) Tim Ream (Centerback)Serginio Dest (R. Wingback) Tyler Adams (Midfield) Malik Tillman (Midfield) Antonee Robinson (L. Wingback)Weston McKennie (Attacking Midfield) Christian Pulisic (Attacking Midfield)Folarin Balogun (Striker) The major change is that Richards, if healthy, comes in for M. Robinson. I am not sure if M. Robinson is Pochettino’s preferred backup over Trusty and McKenzie, but I do expect Richards to start if healthy. It is also possible that Ricardo Pepi or Matt Turner starts at striker or goalkeeper, respectively, but I think those are less likely, but also a less impactful difference. The one thing to note is that Tillman is listed as a holding midfielder rather than as an advanced with, with McKennie taking that advanced role instead. Pochettino actually briefly talked about that in the press conference (the question is in Spanish, but most of the answer is in English). I am under the belief that it was actually an adjustment during the game, where McKennie swapped from playing alongside Adams to higher up the field, with Tillman dropping deeper. As Pochettino mentions, Tillman has experience there at the club level and it showed with a more stable midfield that was more comfortable in possession after a brief Germany squeeze early in the game. In contrast, McKennie brings energy and dynamism to the press along with a more adventurous and attack minded style. In any case, this McKennie, Adams, Tillman (henceforth, the MAT) midfield brought back a lot of that aggressive physicality and pressure that the team seems to have been missing since the last world cup and the peak days of the MMA midfield. title: Coalition of Women Seeking Nominations for Vivian V. Conley Recognition Awards - Muncie Journal
content: MUNCIE, IN — The Muncie-Delaware County Coalition of Women is seeking nominations of local women to honor during the annual Women’s Equality Day Program. The coalition invites nominations of women who have made a significant contribution in the arts, education, religion, business, politics, environment, and social or community service by improving the quality of life in Delaware County. Other categories also will be considered. A letter of nomination of 250 words or fewer describing the nominee’s contributions should be submitted by July 8 to: womensequalitydaymuncie@gmail.com or by mail to ATTN: Women’s Equality Day/YWCA Central Indiana, 310 E. Charles St., Muncie, IN 47305. Recipients will be honored during a program, which will be at 5 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 26, in the Muncie City Hall auditorium. Women’s Equality Day celebrates the passage of the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote. Those being honored will be presented the Vivian V. Conley Recognition Award. Conley, who died May 8, 1993,  was at the forefront of many community issues relating to education, civil rights and aging. She attended Ball State University in her 60s, earning her bachelor’s degree in political science and master’s degree in gerontology. Organizations that make up the coalition are the Friends of Conley, League of Women Voters of Muncie-Delaware County, American Association of University Women, The National Organization for Women, the Indiana Women of Achievement Awards Committee, YWCA Central Indiana and the Coalition of 100 Black Women. “The Women’s Equality Program is important because it shines light on the contributions women make in society, politics, business, civic, and humanitarian efforts,” said WaTasha Barnes Griffin, chief executive officer of YWCA Central Indiana. Additional event details and the honorees will be announced before the event. Sheryl Swingley is a retired Ball State University journalism instructor where she taught for more than 28 years. It is with heavy hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother, Maxine Morris Gordon, on Tuesday June 9, 2026, surrounded by her loving family. Maxine was a woman whose life was defined by love, sacrifice, and unwavering dedication to her family. She spent her life working hard, always putting the needs of others before her own. Whether it was caring for her children, helping raise grandchildren, supporting extended family members, or lending a helping hand to anyone in need, she gave freely of herself without expecting anything in return. Her kindness, strength, and generous spirit touched the lives of everyone who knew her. Family was her greatest joy, and she devoted herself to ensuring those she loved were cared for and supported. The lessons she taught through her actions—love, compassion, perseverance, and selflessness—will continue to live on in the hearts of her family for generations to come. She was proceeded in death by her loving husband, Crawford Franklin "CF" Gordon; father, John Benjamin Morris; mother, Claudia Jenkins Jackson Morris; 4 Brothers, Robert (Bobby) Morris, Gerald (Jerry) Morris, Franklin Morris, and John (Bimbo) Morris; and 2 sisters, Rose Riner, and Grace Turner.
